Around A.D. 372, the Huns entered the lands north of the Euxine, almost exterminating the Alans before crushing the Ostrogoths (PDF p. 61). A Gothic historian describes the Huns as proud, ferocious, and skilled in riding and archery, though possessing shapeless faces (PDF p. 61). The Huns then pressed the Visigoths back to the Danube (PDF p. 61). In A.D. 376, the Visigoths requested permission to cross into the Roman Empire (PDF p. 62). The author judges the Eastern Emperor Valens as stupid, cowardly, and slothful (PDF p. 62). Valens eventually permitted the Goths to settle as subject-allies provided they surrendered their arms and gave hostages (PDF p. 63).

Troubles arose in Moesia when Roman officials accepted bribes to let the Goths retain their weapons (PDF p. 63). The governor, Lupicinus, further provoked the Goths by extorting exorbitant prices for food, which drove some immigrants to sell their children into slavery (PDF p. 63). A conflict between starving Goths and Roman soldiers led Lupicinus to attempt to slay the Goth Fritigern (PDF p. 64). Fritigern escaped and led a year of fighting across the Danube and Balkans (PDF p. 64). While the imperial armies initially held the Visigoths at bay, a battle at Ad Salices proved indecisive (PDF p. 64).

In 378 A.D., Valens personally led an army of 60,000 men to attack the Goths near Adrianople (PDF p. 65). The author notes that the Goths had adopted fighting on horseback while dwelling in the Ukraine (PDF p. 65). During the battle, Gothic cavalry charged the Roman flank, causing the Roman infantry to be packed into a mass where they were cut down (PDF p. 66). Forty thousand Romans fell, including the Emperor (PDF p. 67). The author describes this as the most fearful defeat since Cannae (PDF p. 67). The Goths subsequently attacked Constantinople but retreated after seeing the city's vast walls (PDF p. 67).

By the seventh century, the Latin element in the East was vanishing, partly because the Latin-speaking provinces suffered most from barbarian invasions (PDF p. 169-170). The author reports that Christianity modified social life by ending infanticide and improving the condition of slaves (PDF p. 171-173). However, the author judges that ascetic monasticism became dangerous to the State, as thousands of men retired from civic duties to save their own souls (PDF p. 174-175). This apathetic attitude was viewed by the surviving heathen minority as the ruin of the State (PDF p. 176).
